summary: 'Curiosity' here means careful scrutiny or close examination, not idle interest. A 'moiety' is a portion or share. Gloucester is telling Kent that the two dukes' portions of the kingdom are so precisely balanced that the most careful inspection cannot say which is more valuable.

anchor_text: a son by order of law, some year elder than this
summary: 'By order of law' means legitimate — born inside a legal marriage. Under English common law, a legitimate elder son inherited his father's titles and estate; a bastard son had no legal claim at all. Gloucester's casual disclosure that his legitimate son Edgar is only marginally older than his illegitimate Edmund — and that he regards them with equal affection — plants the resentment Edmund will act on.

anchor_text: He hath been out nine years, and away he shall again
summary: Edmund has been living abroad ('out'), away from his father's household, for nine years and is about to be sent away again. Sending a bastard son overseas — to an army, to a foreign court, to school on the continent — was standard practice among Elizabethan gentry who lacked a settled place for such children at home. Gloucester's casual dismissal of Edmund in the same sentence that introduces him to Kent reinforces Edmund's grievance.

anchor_text: Give me the map there.--Know that we have divided In three our kingdom
summary: Lear produces a physical map and announces he has already divided Britain into three portions — one for each daughter and her husband. The map makes the partition a visible, theatrical act: the kingdom is something that can be cut up and handed out. To a Jacobean audience who knew King James I was pressing Parliament to unite England and Scotland into one 'Great Britain,' a king dividing a unified island into three pieces would have read as a self-evident disaster.
detail: The map prop has no precedent in Geoffrey of Monmouth or Holinshed: Shakespeare adds it to literalize the abstraction of political division. In legal and political theory the kingdom was the body politic — an indivisible whole. Breaking it apart for a family love-contest collapses the distinction between a king's public office and his private paternal feelings, the error that will unravel everything. The Jacobean resonance with James's Union project (proposed 1604, still being debated as the play was written c. 1605-6) is pointed: where James tried to make two kingdoms one, Lear makes one kingdom three.

sources.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)

The map-as-theatrical-literalization and the two-bodies point are sound, but the Jacobean resonance with James I's Union project is a plausible scholarly argument that is not universally accepted as authorial intent; the annotation presents it as pointed fact rather than a contested interpretive claim, which slightly overreaches.

anchor_text: Our daughters' several dowers, that future strife May be prevented now
summary: 'Several' means separate or respective (each daughter's own portion). A 'dower' was the land or property settled on a bride as part of the marriage arrangement; here Lear is assigning the kingdom itself as dowry. By announcing all three shares now, he hopes to forestall quarrels after his death. The irony is that his announcement produces the catastrophe it was meant to prevent.

anchor_text: we will divest us both of rule, Interest of territory, cares of state
summary: 'Divest' means to strip off, as one takes off a garment. Lear proposes to remove from himself the actual power of kingship — governance, territory, administration. 'Interest of territory' means legal title to the land. The play's defining tragedy is that Lear tries to give away the substance of kingship while keeping its symbols; the theory that a king has two inseparable bodies — the natural man and the undying royal office — holds that such a separation is impossible.
detail: Tudor legal and political theory, most famously articulated in Edmund Plowden's Commentaries (c. 1571) and later analysed by Kantorowicz in The King's Two Bodies (1957), held that the royal dignity could not be stripped from the person of the king — the two 'bodies' were one. Lear's attempt to perform exactly this split — 'The sway, / Revenue, execution of the rest, / Beloved sons, be yours; which to confirm, / This coronet part betwixt you' — is the foundational error from which everything else follows. He will shortly discover that without the office there is no 'king' for others to honour.

sources.name: Plowden, Commentaries

Lear's description of Goneril's third as forests, open plains, rivers, and meadows is a miniature geography of Britain's landscape types, making the division concrete and territorial.

anchor_text: the most precious square of sense possesses, And find I am alone felicitate
summary: The 'most precious square of sense' means all the faculties of perception taken together — sight, hearing, taste, smell, touch — as a complete, perfectly formed whole ('square' can mean something perfectly proportioned or complete). 'Felicitate' is an adjective here meaning made happy, blissful. Regan claims that only Lear's love makes her fully happy; everything her senses could enjoy is worthless without it.

anchor_text: Nothing can come of nothing: speak again
summary: Lear's retort echoes the ancient philosophical axiom 'ex nihilo nihil fit' — from nothing, nothing comes — used from the pre-Socratic philosopher Lucretius onward to argue that creation requires matter. Lear deploys it as a commercial threat: nothing offered in the love-test earns nothing back. But Cordelia's 'nothing' is the only honest answer in the scene, which means Lear's axiom destroys the one relationship he cannot afford to lose.
detail: The formula goes back to Parmenides (c. 5th century BCE) and is central to Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.149-156 ('nullam rem e nihilo gigni divinitus umquam' — no thing is ever produced by divine power out of nothing). Shakespeare reaches for it at the play's first great crisis, letting a logical-sounding principle serve an irrational anger. The Fool will later remind Lear that by giving everything away he has made himself a 'nothing' — turning the axiom on its maker. The word 'nothing' recurs obsessively through the play as its key note of negation and loss.

sources.name: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura
sources.citation: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.149-156 (ex nihilo nihil fit; the Epicurean axiom that nothing is produced from nothing).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 86

Lucretius, De Rerum Natura 1.149-150 does contain 'nullam rem e nihilo gigni divinitus umquam'; the line range 1.149-156 is a slight extension of the actual two-line statement but falls within the same passage; the Epicurean axiom and its pre-Socratic ancestry are accurately described.

The echo of ex nihilo nihil fit (Parmenides via Lucretius) is a mainstream scholarly identification; the note attributing it specifically to Lucretius 1.149-156 is accurate, and the reading that Lear misapplies a logical axiom against the one honest voice is sound.

anchor_text: I love your majesty According to my bond; no more nor less
summary: 'Bond' means the natural obligation that binds a child to a parent — the duty owed by virtue of the relationship itself, not additional to it. Cordelia is not being cold; she is saying she loves Lear exactly as much as a daughter is bound to love a father, which is to say genuinely and completely. The play's tragedy hinges on Lear's inability to hear 'bond' as a word of love rather than a legal minimum.
detail: The word 'bond' carries a double resonance: a legal binding document and a natural tie of kinship and duty. Cordelia means the latter — the natural love that goes with the relationship itself, as she explains in lines 93-101. Edmund, in 1.2, will pervert the word in the opposite direction, framing his natural 'bond' to his father as something he owes nothing to. The contrast between genuine bonds (Cordelia, Kent, Edgar) and broken ones (Edmund, Goneril, Regan) structures the whole play.

anchor_text: That lord whose hand must take my plight shall carry Half my love with him, half my care and duty
summary: 'Plight' here means a solemn pledge or faith — specifically, the troth-plight of betrothal or marriage, when two people pledge their hands and faith to each other. Cordelia is saying that when she marries, her husband will rightfully claim half the love she now gives entirely to her father. This is theologically and legally orthodox — Ephesians 5:31 and the marriage service both held that a wife cleaves to her husband — but Lear, who has confused private paternal love with royal entitlement, cannot accept it.

anchor_text: by the sacred radiance of the sun, The mysteries of Hecate, and the night; By all the operation of the orbs
summary: Lear swears by three pagan powers: the sun, Hecate (the Greek goddess of magic and night), and the influence of the heavenly bodies (planets and stars). The play is set in a pre-Christian, pagan Britain, so characters invoke gods of nature and the heavens rather than the Christian God. This triple oath — sky, underworld goddess, and the stars — is a solemn, cosmic form of cursing Cordelia.

Lear is doing something that Elizabethans would have recognized as legally and morally impossible: a father cannot simply dissolve the natural bond with his child by declaring it void.

anchor_text: The barbarous Scythian, Or he that makes his generation messes To gorge his appetite
summary: The Scythians were nomadic peoples of the Eurasian steppe who, in ancient Greek and Roman writing, were the archetype of savagery — the farthest-flung, most uncivilized people imaginable. Ancient sources also attributed to certain peoples (sometimes the Scythians, sometimes Thyestean figures in myth) the cannibalistic eating of their own offspring. Lear is saying that even such a monster — who eats his own children — will be closer to his heart than Cordelia.
detail: Classical authors from Herodotus onward cited Scythian customs as markers of barbarism; Shakespeare's audience would have recognized them as the ultimate distant savages, opposed to civilization. The 'eating one's generation' detail gestures at the mythic banquets of Thyestes and Tantalus (fathers/grandfathers who ate their own children), traditions available through Seneca and Ovid. The hyperbole measures the ferocity of Lear's rage and, in retrospect, its grotesque irrationality.

sources.citation: Herodotus, Histories 4.1-82 (the Scythians as the most remote and savage of peoples, the classical archetype of barbarism).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 114

The Scythians as the classical archetype of savagery is accurate (Herodotus and many others), and the gesture toward Thyestes-type cannibal-of-offspring myths is a mainstream scholarly parallel; the hyperbole reading is sound.

anchor_text: Come not between the dragon and his wrath
summary: The dragon was the heraldic emblem of the ancient kings of Britain: the Red Dragon, still the symbol of Wales today, was the standard of the legendary Brutus and the British kings his line produced — the lineage in which the Lear legend places the king. Lear calling himself 'the dragon' is a claim of legendary British royal identity, not merely a figure for his anger.
detail: Geoffrey of Monmouth, whose Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136) is the ultimate source of the Lear legend, placed the kings of Britain in descent from Brutus of Troy; their heraldic symbol was the dragon. Holinshed and Tudor heraldry preserved the association. Shakespeare is precise: Lear does not say 'come not between the lion and his wrath' (the English royal arms), but 'dragon' — the specifically British royal beast for this pre-Roman, legendary story. The choice grounds the play in the mythic-British world of its sources.

sources.name: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae
sources.citation: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae (c. 1136), on the legendary kings of Britain descended from Brutus of Troy and the dragon as their emblem.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 121

While the dragon is indeed associated with legendary British kings via Geoffrey of Monmouth and Tudor heraldry, the claim that Lear's use of 'dragon' is a precise heraldic choice distinguishing British from English royal iconography (lion vs. dragon) is an interpretive inference rather than a textually secure claim; it is defensible but may overstate authorial precision.

anchor_text: I lov'd her most, and thought to set my rest On her kind nursery
summary: 'Set my rest' is a phrase from the card game primero: to stake everything on a single hand, making one's final stand. 'Nursery' means tender care, the act of nursing the aged — Lear had planned to live out his days cared for by Cordelia. The gambling image is precise: he wagered his comfort on a love-test and lost.

anchor_text: I do invest you jointly in my power, Pre-eminence, and all the large effects That troop with majesty
summary: 'The large effects that troop with majesty' means the outward signs of royal authority that accompany kingship — armed retinue, ceremony, precedence, obedience from subjects. Lear is handing over the real instruments of power to Cornwall and Albany. In the very next breath he declares he will keep 'the name and all the additions to a king' — the title — but without the substance. Kent will call this madness.
detail: The list of what Lear keeps and what he gives away stages the 'two bodies' problem dramatically. 'Revenue, execution of the rest' means tax income and the power to enforce law — the financial and coercive foundations of royal authority. A 'name' without these is, as the Fool later puts it, an 'O without a figure' — a zero. The political logic is exactly what the play's subsequent action demonstrates: the name of king without its powers invites contempt.

anchor_text: The name, and all the additions to a king
summary: 'Additions' are the titles and honorific styles that identify a person's rank — 'King', 'Your Majesty', and all their ceremonial equivalents. Lear believes he can retain the dignity of kingship after surrendering its power. Tudor political theory held this was a contradiction: the royal title was inseparable from the royal office and its capacities. The play dramatizes the theory by showing Lear progressively stripped even of the 'additions' he thought he could keep.
detail: Edmund Plowden's legal doctrine of the king's two bodies held that the body politic — the office, dignity, and power of the crown — was immortal and inseparable from the man who held it while he held it. Lear's attempted split, and his subsequent loss of even the 'name' as his daughters strip him of his knights and refuse him shelter, dramatizes what the doctrine predicted: you cannot be king by name alone. The word 'additions' recurs in Lear and in Coriolanus to mark the titles given or taken away as markers of political identity.

sources.name: Plowden, Commentaries

Plowden's Commentaries do contain the doctrine that the body politic is inseparable from the king's person while he holds office, and Kantorowicz (1957) is the standard analysis; both citations are real and directly supportive.

The reading that 'additions' are honorific titles and that Lear's attempt to retain the dignity without the power dramatizes the Plowden/Kantorowicz two-bodies doctrine is mainstream; the point that the play demonstrates Lear losing even the 'name' is textually supported.

anchor_text: This coronet part betwixt you
summary: A coronet is a small crown worn by nobles below the rank of monarch; it is not the royal crown itself. Lear hands a ducal coronet — the token of Cordelia's share of the kingdom — to Cornwall and Albany to split. The act of dividing a crown between two men on stage is a visual symbol of the sundering of the kingdom, and Cornwall and Albany exchange an awkward silence before Kent speaks: neither takes it. The staging literalizes what is being broken.

anchor_text: The bow is bent and drawn; make from the shaft
summary: 'Make from the shaft' means get out of the path of the arrow — stand aside before it is released. Lear is warning Kent to back off: the decision is made and the shot is about to be fired. Kent refuses, saying he would rather take the arrow through the heart than abandon honest service. The image of an unstoppable projectile recurs as a metaphor for Lear's irrevocable judgments throughout the scene.

anchor_text: Thou, nature, art my goddess; to thy law

summary: Gloucester reads the family crisis and the kingdom's disorder as symptoms of celestial warnings. 'Late eclipses' refers to real events: a lunar eclipse in September 1605 and a solar eclipse in October 1605 had been widely reported and interpreted as omens of political disaster. Elizabethan and Jacobean astrology held that eclipses signalled disruptions in the social order — exactly the catalogue Gloucester gives: 'love cools, friendship falls off, brothers divide: in cities, mutinies; in countries, discord; in palaces, treason; and the bond cracked twixt son and father.'
detail: Astrology was not fringe belief in Shakespeare's England; it was mainstream natural philosophy, taught at universities. A disruption in the heavens was thought to propagate downward through the chain of being into every level of society and nature. The 1605 eclipses were widely reported in almanacs and prognostications, making Gloucester's speech topical. The phrase 'wisdom of nature can reason it thus and thus' (TLN 417) acknowledges that the natural philosophers (astronomers and philosophers of nature) can provide technical explanations for eclipses, yet insists the resulting social catastrophes are real whatever the explanation. Edmund's scornful response moments later will give the opposing, sceptical view.

anchor_text: This is the excellent foppery of the world, that, when we are sick in fortune
summary: 'Foppery' here means foolishness or credulity, not foppishness in dress. Edmund's soliloquy is a sustained attack on fatalism: people who blame their failures on the stars are making an 'admirable evasion' — a magnificent excuse — for their own bad behaviour. 'Whoremaster man' means man as a lecher, governed by lust; 'goatish disposition' tags lust specifically, since goats were proverbially lascivious. Edmund's point is that a man who was himself conceived in lust calls his lust the stars' fault.
detail: Edmund's speech voices what historians of ideas call the 'providentialist vs. naturalist' debate: is human life shaped by cosmic forces, or is character the product of the individual's own choices? He comes down decisively on the self-determining side, which aligns with the anti-fatalist strain in contemporary sceptical thought. The irony is structural: Edmund has just been set up, in the play's logic, as an agent of exactly the disorders Gloucester blamed on the eclipses. Whether the play endorses Edmund's rationalism or shows it as itself a form of dangerous self-deception is one of the central interpretive questions of the text.

anchor_text: knaves, thieves, and treachers by spherical pre-dominance; drunkards, liars, and adulterers by an enforced obedience of planetary influence
summary: 'Spherical pre-dominance' is technical astrological language: each of the seven planetary spheres (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) was held to govern a particular region of the sky at any given moment and to exert power — 'predominance' — over human character and action. Edmund is mocking the logic by which a drunk can blame his drunkenness on whichever planet happened to be dominant at his birth.
detail: Renaissance cosmology inherited from Ptolemy a model of concentric spheres, each carrying a planet, rotating around the earth. An astrologer could calculate which planet 'pre-dominated' — held power in the ascendant — at any moment, and use this to explain or predict temperament and events. 'Treachers' is an archaic form of 'traitors' (OED s.v. 'treacher'). Edmund's catalogue — knave, thief, traitor, drunkard, liar, adulterer — deliberately names the worst moral failures so that the absurdity of blaming them on a planet is as glaring as possible. 'An admirable evasion of whoremaster man' (TLN 436) means a wonderfully convenient escape from responsibility.

anchor_text: on whose foolish honesty / My practices ride easy!
summary: 'Practices' here means scheming plots and machinations — not innocent activities. Edmund closes the scene by congratulating himself that Gloucester's credulity and Edgar's honest nature make his plots easy to execute. The closing couplet ('Let me, if not by birth, have lands by wit: / All with me's meet that I can fashion fit') is a formal declaration of the stage Machiavel's creed: what matters is not inherited right but the ability to scheme, and everything is legitimate if it can be made to serve his purpose.
detail: The word 'practices' in Shakespeare consistently carries the sense of secret, dishonest scheming (OED s.v. 'practice' n. sense 6); it appears in the same sense in Othello, Macbeth, and elsewhere. Edmund's closing couplet rhyming 'wit' and 'fit' sounds almost proverbial — a neat, worldly-wise maxim — which makes his villainy attractive rather than repellent, a defining feature of the stage Machiavel. The soliloquy is the mirror-image of the opening one: he began by invoking the world as it is (biological force without sentiment), and he ends by announcing that he will use cunning to take what birth denied. The rhyme closes the scene on a note of settled, cheerful ruthlessness.

anchor_text: If you come slack of former services, / You shall do well
summary: The syntax is deliberately inverted. Goneril means: if Oswald and the household staff do their jobs worse than before — slacking off on the service they used to provide Lear — that slackness is exactly what she wants, and she will answer for any blame. 'Come slack of' means fall short of, and 'you shall do well' means you will please me, not you will perform well.
detail: The inversion captures Goneril's political strategy: she wants to provoke Lear into a confrontation she can then use against him, and she is directing her steward to engineer that provocation by withdrawal of ordinary deference. 'The fault of it I'll answer' means she will take responsibility for the deliberate neglect — a notable moment, since it shows premeditation, not irritation. Editors from Malone onward have noted the compressed, almost businesslike syntax as characteristic of Goneril's speaking style throughout the early acts.

anchor_text: Idle old man, / That still would manage those authorities / That he hath given away
summary: 'Idle' here means foolish or useless, not lazy. 'Still' means 'continues to' (the older sense). 'Authorities' means the powers of government — decrees, commands, control over the household — that Lear handed to his daughters in Act 1 Scene 1. Goneril's complaint is that Lear keeps trying to exercise a royal authority he has legally surrendered.
detail: This speech makes explicit the political contradiction at the heart of the play's first movement: Lear gave away his 'darker purpose' (the substance of kingship) but kept 'the name, and all the addition to a king' (1.1). Goneril sees only the absurdity of a man who has divested himself of power yet still acts as though he holds it. The doctrine of the king's two bodies is relevant here: Lear has separated his 'body natural' from his 'body politic,' and the result is a figure who is neither a functioning ruler nor a private person. Goneril's contemptuous label 'Idle old man' collapses the political problem into a personal insult — but she is also, in a narrowly legal sense, correct that the authorities have been given away.

anchor_text: Old fools are babes again; and must be us'd / With checks as flatteries
summary: Goneril inverts a proverb about the second childhood of old age. 'Checks' means rebukes or corrections. 'When they are seen abus'd' means when old people are shown to have been misled by flattery. Her logic: flattery has made Lear behave badly ('abus'd' = corrupted by indulgence), so he must now be disciplined with sharp rebukes ('checks') the way a misbehaving infant is corrected — not coddled further.
detail: The rhetorical compression is deliberately brutal. A commonplace of Renaissance moral writing held that very old men revert to a child's dependence and need to be humored (compare Jaques's 'second childishness' in As You Like It 2.7). Goneril takes this familiar idea and twists it: instead of the expected conclusion (therefore treat them gently), she argues the opposite (therefore correct them sharply). The shift from 'flatteries' to 'checks' also describes the policy she has just ordered — replacing Oswald's former deference with deliberate cold neglect. 'Abus'd' carries its older meaning of deceived or misled, implying Lear has been corrupted by a lifetime of sycophancy.

anchor_text: I would breed from hence occasions, and I shall, / That I may speak
summary: 'Breed from hence occasions' means deliberately create opportunities — manufacture pretexts for a confrontation. Goneril is not waiting for Lear to overstep; she is engineering the conditions that will force a clash, so she will have justification to speak openly against him. The plan she outlines here (cold household, a letter to Regan, a coming confrontation) is premeditated, not reactive.
detail: 'Occasion' in Elizabethan English meant a convenient opportunity or, more specifically, a justifying cause for action — the thing that licenses one to do or say what one already intends. 'Breed' in the sense of bring forth, generate, underlines the calculated nature of the plan: Goneril will cultivate grievances the way one breeds livestock, until they are large enough to use. The phrase is a compressed statement of her strategy for the next two acts: make Lear's retinue and behavior intolerable, accumulate legitimate-seeming complaints, and strip him further. Writing to Regan confirms that the two sisters have already agreed on the broad outline of their policy.

anchor_text: to eat no fish
summary: In Elizabethan England, eating fish on Fridays and in Lent was associated with Catholic practice; Protestants who wanted to signal their faith sometimes ostentatiously refused fish. Kent's boast that he eats 'no fish' was a quick audience shorthand for: I am a sound, plain Protestant Englishman. The play is nominally set in pagan Britain, so the joke is an anachronism — but the audience would catch it immediately.
detail: The fish-day associations had become a point of Protestant self-identification; a man who loudly ate no fish on Fridays was advertising loyalty to the reformed church. Some editors also propose a bawdy secondary meaning, but the historical-Protestant sense is sufficient and more widely cited.

anchor_text: Truth's a dog must to kennel; he must be whipped out, when the lady brach may stand by the fire and stink

The Fool is commenting on his own situation: he tells Lear truth and risks the whip; the fawning Goneril sits close to the warmth of power.

anchor_text: Have more than thou showest, Speak less than thou knowest
summary: The Fool delivers a rhyming catalogue of prudential maxims — spend less than you have, lend less than you possess, gamble cautiously ('set less than thou throwest'), avoid women and drink, stay home — and then deflates the whole thing: follow all this advice and you gain nothing ('more than two tens to a score' = nothing beyond twenty). The jingle is a parody of proverbial wisdom. Its point is that Lear did the opposite of every one of these cautions when he gave his kingdom away.

The couplet-by-couplet structure imitates the verse form of popular wisdom literature, then undermines it with the punchline that even perfect prudence gets you nowhere — the counsel is useless after the damage is done.

anchor_text: nothing can be made out of nothing
summary: Lear repeats an axiom of classical and scholastic natural philosophy: ex nihilo nihil fit — from nothing, nothing comes. The philosophical tag becomes a prophecy of Lear's own destitution.

anchor_text: if I had a monopoly out, they would have part on't and loads too
summary: A 'monopoly' was a royal grant giving one person or company exclusive right to trade in a particular commodity. Elizabeth I granted many such monopolies as a form of patronage; in the Parliament of 1601 they caused a major controversy, with MPs attacking them as extortionate privileges that cornered the market in everyday goods like starch, salt, and playing cards. The Fool jokes that even his exclusive right to be a fool would be seized by the lords and great men — a pointed joke about royal favouritism.
detail: The 1601 debate on monopolies was fresh in the minds of Shakespeare's first audiences; Elizabeth famously promised reform. The Fool's gag uses a sore political topic to accuse the court of hoarding all available folly — a meta-joke that calls the lords themselves fools.

anchor_text: thou clovest thy crown i' the middle and gav'st away both parts, thou borest thine ass on thy back

Lear has inverted nature: he is now dependent on those who should depend on him.

anchor_text: this your all-licens'd fool

anchor_text: Doth any here know me?--This is not Lear
summary: Lear's question to the assembled court is half rhetorical outrage, half genuine existential crisis: if his daughter can treat him this way, he must no longer be the Lear he was. His self-questioning — 'Doth Lear walk thus? speak thus? Where are his eyes?' — reaches the terrifying centre of his situation: he gave his authority away and is discovering he cannot retrieve the self that authority made him. The Fool's answer, 'Lear's shadow,' is the play's most economical formulation of this loss.

anchor_text: Hear, nature, hear; dear goddess, hear
summary: Lear prays not to a Christian God but to Nature as a goddess — consistent with the play's deliberately pagan ancient-British setting. Nature in this context is both the cosmic force that orders the world and the deity who governs reproduction and generation. His invocation of her against his own daughter is also an invocation of the natural order she governs: a daughter who defies a father has defied Nature herself, and Lear calls Nature's power to ratify the curse.
detail: The play's characters swear by pagan deities — Hecate, Jupiter, Apollo, Nature — never by the Christian God, maintaining the pre-Roman British setting throughout. anchor_text: she's as like this as a crab's like an apple
summary: A 'crab' here is a crab-apple — the small, wild, intensely sour variety of apple. The Fool appears to say Regan resembles Goneril only slightly, the way a crab-apple resembles a regular apple (same shape, but very different taste). Then he undercuts even that: Regan will taste to Lear exactly as a crab does to a crab — meaning both daughters are equally sour and bitter, whatever the superficial difference. The repeated 'crab' locks in the implication: there is no sweet apple among Lear's children now.
detail: The crab-apple was the native wild English apple — small, hard, and astringent, inedible raw. Elizabethan writers used 'crab' as a shorthand for sourness or shrewishness; Petruchio in The Taming of the Shrew calls Katharina 'my super-dainty Kate, for dainties are all crabbes' (2.1). The Fool's double use of 'crab' — first as a simile of resemblance ('as a crab's like an apple'), then in a repetition that collapses the difference ('as a crab does to a crab') — is characteristic of his verbal strategy: he seems to offer consolation only to retract it. Lear's aside 'I did her wrong' (TLN 866), breaking off from the Fool's jest, suggests the joke is landing.

anchor_text: the reason why the seven stars are no more than seven
summary: The 'seven stars' is a common name for the Pleiades, a star cluster in the constellation Taurus. Seven stars are visible to the naked eye in clear conditions, and the cluster was widely used for navigation and for marking the farming calendar. The Fool's riddle — why are there only seven? — has no real answer, which is the point: Lear's straight-faced reply ('Because they are not eight') is perfectly circular and logically empty, prompting the Fool to say Lear would make a good fool. The exchange is the scene's clearest statement that Lear's judgment has become as tautological as a fool's.
detail: The Pleiades were known as the 'seven stars' in everyday English; Shakespeare uses the name in 1 Henry IV (1.2) and The Two Gentlemen of Verona as a commonplace. The cluster is actually more than seven stars, but antiquity and tradition fixed the number at seven. In classical mythology the Pleiades were the seven daughters of Atlas, transformed into stars — Ovid tells the story in the Fasti (4.169-178) and Metamorphoses (13.293). Lear's literal-minded non-answer ('because they are not eight') mimics the form of a logical answer while saying nothing — a fool's trick, which is the Fool's entire point about the kind of wit Lear has been showing.

anchor_text: The better! best! This weaves itself perforce
summary: Edmund is alone on stage and speaks directly to himself (and effectively to the audience) in rapid, clipped phrases. The climbing exclamations -- 'The better! best!' -- show his mind accelerating as he sees Cornwall's arrival as an unexpected gift for his scheme. 'Perforce' means 'by necessity' or 'without effort on my part'; the plot is weaving itself for him.
detail: This short soliloquy is a hallmark of the stage Machiavel: the villain who confides gleefully in the audience, relishing how events conspire in his favour. Edmund has just been told that Cornwall -- the powerful duke he hopes to serve -- is arriving tonight, exactly when he needs a high-ranking witness to his false story against Edgar. The phrase 'weaves itself' attributes agency to fortune rather than to Edmund, a momentary irony from a character who elsewhere scorns fortune and claims to make his own destiny.

anchor_text: the revenging gods 'Gainst parricides did all their thunders bend
summary: Edmund claims he warned Edgar that the gods direct their thunderbolts specifically against parricides -- people who murder a parent. 'Parricide' (killing one's own father or parent) was the ultimate crime in Roman law and in Elizabethan moral thought, punishable by special divine wrath. The irony is sharp: Edmund himself is plotting his father's destruction.
detail: The pagan British world of King Lear has no Christian God; its characters swear by Jupiter, Apollo, and unnamed 'gods,' and they attribute both punishment and providence to these pagan powers. In Roman law parricide was a special category of crime punished in a distinctive way (the sack, or poena cullei, in which the offender was sewn into a sack with animals and thrown into the sea). The thunder as a divine weapon against the wicked is a commonplace of the play's pagan theology -- Lear later calls on the gods to strike down his daughters' ingratitude with thunder. Edmund's invocation of divine punishment against parricides is exactly calculated to trigger Gloucester's deepest fears about Edgar, while concealing that it is Edmund who plans the equivalent crime: destroying his father.

anchor_text: Thou unpossessing bastard! dost thou think, If I would stand against thee, would the reposal Of any trust
summary: Edmund quotes the words Edgar supposedly threw at him. 'Unpossessing bastard' means a bastard who cannot legally hold or inherit property -- under English law illegitimate children could not inherit real estate. 'Reposal of any trust' means the placing of confidence or belief -- Edgar (in Edmund's fabrication) is saying no one would believe the word of a bastard with nothing to lose.
detail: The legal status of bastards was a live issue in early modern England: illegitimate children were 'nullius filius' ('son of nobody') in law, unable to inherit land, hold offices, or give evidence against a legitimate heir. This is the real wound Edmund's character has spent the play seething over. In 1.2 he explicitly names the 'plague of custom' and the 'curiosity of nations' that deprive him of his brother's share. By having 'Edgar' hurl the word back at him -- 'unpossessing bastard' -- Edmund both reports a plausible insult and stages his own grievance for Gloucester to witness, sharpening Gloucester's sympathy for the 'wronged' Edmund.

anchor_text: though thou didst produce My very character

anchor_text: All ports I'll bar
summary: Gloucester plans to close all sea-ports so Edgar cannot flee the kingdom. In Shakespeare's England a royal proclamation could close ports to prevent a fugitive or traitor escaping -- this is a real administrative power Gloucester claims he can exercise with Cornwall's authority. The measure was used against actual state enemies in the Tudor and early Stuart period.

Gloucester here signals his intention to treat Edgar as a traitor subject to the full machinery of state. The detail also plants a dramatic irony: Edgar is already well inland, hiding in the play's landscape, not at sea -- the ports-order is both tyrannically comprehensive and theatrically irrelevant to where Edgar actually is. By placing 'All ports I'll bar' immediately after the trumpets announce Cornwall's arrival, Shakespeare links the two: it is Cornwall's authority that will give Gloucester's proclamation force.

anchor_text: natural boy, I'll work the means To make thee capable
summary: Both words here carry legal weight. 'Natural boy' does not mean genuine or sincere -- it is a common Elizabethan term for an illegitimate child (a 'natural son,' born in nature but outside lawful wedlock). 'Make thee capable' means make you legally able to inherit -- to overcome the legal bar that bastards faced in inheriting real property and titles. Gloucester is promising to find a way to legitimise Edmund's inheritance rights.
detail: The cruel irony saturates the moment: Gloucester's deepest paternal gift -- the promise to break through the legal barrier that Edmund has been seething about since his opening soliloquy -- is being offered to the very son who has just engineered the ruin of the legitimate heir. In English law, inheritance by a bastard required either an act of Parliament or a specific royal dispensation; there was no simple private remedy. Gloucester's vow is thus both sincere and probably empty. Edmund must have savoured it. 'Natural' as a term for illegitimate appears across the canon (the 'natural son' of Edmund's own opening speech in 1.2: 'Why bastard? wherefore base?') and reflects the period's vocabulary for birth outside marriage.

anchor_text: I had thee in Lipsbury pinfold
summary: A pinfold is a pound — an enclosure where stray animals were locked up until their owner paid a fine to recover them. 'Lipsbury' is probably a fictitious place-name invented by Kent, punning on 'lips' (i.e., between my teeth), meaning: if I had you penned in between my jaws, I would make you pay attention to me.
detail: No real place called Lipsbury is on record. Editors from Johnson onward have glossed 'Lipsbury' as a jocular coinage from 'lip,' so 'Lipsbury pinfold' = 'the pound of my mouth' — a threat to bite, or simply a vivid insult for a painful grip. The pinfold metaphor is appropriate: Oswald is being called an animal who needs to be caught and impounded. Kent's speech throughout the scene deploys a rush of precise, contemptuous vocabulary designed to overwhelm and humiliate, and this opening volley sets the tone.

anchor_text: eater of broken meats
summary: 'Broken meats' are the scraps and leftovers from a meal — the portions swept off the table after the family and honoured guests have eaten. To call Oswald an 'eater of broken meats' is to place him at the bottom of a great house's hierarchy, living off what others leave behind, a creature of dependence with no dignity of his own.
detail: In Elizabethan and Jacobean households, food moved strictly by rank: the lord and his family ate first, then the upper servants, then the lower servants — broken meats were the scrapings that reached the lowest rungs. As Goneril's steward Oswald is a functionary of the household, not a gentleman; Kent's insult places him below even that status and introduces the extended accusation of servility that follows.

anchor_text: three-suited, hundred-pound, filthy, worsted-stocking knave

'Hundred-pound' marks him as barely a gentleman by Elizabethan property standards (a gentleman typically needed at least that income per year, a marginal threshold). anchor_text: take vanity the puppet's part against the royalty of her father
summary: Kent is accusing Oswald of carrying letters from Goneril that act against King Lear's authority. 'Vanity' here means an empty, false, morally worthless show — the same word used for the Vice-character in morality plays. 'The puppet's part' means playing the role of a mere puppet or marionette: Oswald is doing Goneril's bidding like a mechanical figure with no will of his own, and the 'vanity' he serves is her hollow self-interest set against her father's rightful kingship.
detail: In Tudor morality plays and popular pageants, 'Vanity' was often a personified vice-character, a hollow theatrical figure. Kent's phrase fuses the morality-play sense (Oswald serves moral emptiness personified) with the puppet image (he is a mindless instrument). The contrast with 'royalty of her father' is sharp: Lear still holds royal authority, and to work against that on behalf of mere Vanity is treachery. The insult also extends the sustained attack on Oswald's servility — he is not even an agent, just a prop that Goneril animates.

anchor_text: I'll so carbonado your shanks
summary: To carbonado meat is to score it across with a knife before grilling or broiling — scoring shallow cuts into it so it cooks through. Kent is threatening to hack Oswald's legs (shanks) with his sword as if preparing a cut of meat for the fire. The word turns Oswald into a piece of butcher's stock, reducing him to something less than human.
detail: A carbonado (from Italian carbonata, related to carbone, charcoal) was a culinary technique: meat or fish was gashed repeatedly across the surface, sometimes rubbed with salt, then grilled. The word appears in Elizabethan cookery writing. Shakespeare uses it twice in the corpus: here and in All's Well That Ends Well (4.5), both times as a cooking threat that likens a man to raw meat. Combined with 'shanks' — a butcher's term for the lower leg of a carcass — it strips all pretension from the target and fits the scene's wider presentation of Oswald as less than human.

anchor_text: I'll flesh you; come on, young master
summary: To 'flesh' a hound, hawk, or young soldier meant to give it its first taste of real flesh — to blood it in its first kill, so as to excite and train it for future combat. Kent is mockingly offering to give Edmund his first real fight, addressing him as an untried youth ('young master') who has never been properly blooded. The insult implies Edmund is still too green to be taken seriously.
detail: The term was in active use for breaking in hunting animals: a hound was 'fleshed' on its first quarry to stir its blood-lust. Applied to a soldier or fighter, it meant giving him his first real taste of violence. The Folio and Quarto texts agree on 'flesh.' Edmund has just entered the scene and not yet drawn; Kent immediately marks him as a novice. This is the same Kent who has moments earlier been trying to provoke Oswald; he simply transfers his aggression, undeterred by the arrival of the noble party.

anchor_text: nature disclaims in thee; a tailor made thee
summary: Kent's logic is: nature (the force that creates genuine human character) washes its hands of Oswald — he has no natural substance, no real inner man. What made him was a tailor, because he is nothing but an outer garment, a dressed-up costume with no body inside. The insult says that Oswald exists only as a social surface: his identity is purely the livery he wears in Goneril's service.
detail: The idea that a person is made only of their clothes — that fine dress can construct a counterfeit person where no genuine one exists — is a recurring satirical motif in the period. The joke appears elsewhere in Shakespeare: in Macbeth (2.4) and in Measure for Measure (2.2) clothing is used to probe the gap between office and virtue. Here it answers Oswald's charge that Kent is an 'ancient ruffian': Kent's point is that Oswald's smooth presentation conceals an absence of worth. Cornwall's confused reply ('Thou art a strange fellow: a tailor make a man?') lets Kent sharpen the insult: a stonecutter or painter, who work in solid or visible materials, could not have produced something as shoddy as Oswald.

anchor_text: thou whoreson zed! thou unnecessary letter
summary: Kent bursts out calling Oswald 'zed' — the letter Z — and 'unnecessary,' because Z was the last and least letter of the English alphabet, omitted from many Latin grammars as superfluous (since S could do its work). To call a person a Z was to say they were the most dispensable, lowest-ranked item in the whole order of things. The insult is a comic flash of learned wit in the middle of the brawl.
detail: Z was regularly dropped from Latin grammars used in Tudor schools — for example, William Lily's standard Latin grammar (the official text in use since Henry VIII's reign) omitted it, and even English spelling guides noted it was rarely needed. For an Elizabethan schoolboy — and Shakespeare, like Kent, was schooled in Lily — 'the unnecessary Z' was a genuine classroom memory. The insult works on two levels: it is scholarly (Kent knows Latin grammar) and it precisely positions Oswald as the most useless element of any available system. The outburst also interrupts Oswald's condescending account of having 'spared' Kent because of his grey beard, and Kent's fury at that condescension intensifies the schoolmasterly insult.

anchor_text: bite the holy cords a-twain / Which are too intrinse t' unloose
summary: 'Holy cords' are the sacred bonds of natural relationship — the ties between parent and child, husband and wife, lord and subject. 'A-twain' means in two, severed. 'Intrinse' (or 'intrince') is an archaic form of 'intrinsic' meaning too tightly knotted to be undone by hand. Kent is saying that flatterers like Oswald gnaw through ties that are too tightly twisted to be properly untied — they destroy bonds that should be permanent by the sheer corrosive work of smooth complicity.
detail: The image is densely compressed. The 'holy cords' that smooth flatterers bite apart are the natural moral bonds that hold society together — parent-child and lord-subject most prominently, the very bonds the play dramatizes being destroyed. 'Too intrinse t' unloose' acknowledges the paradox: bonds so tight they cannot be properly dissolved are being severed by underhanded means rather than legitimate ones. The Quarto reads 'intrinse,' the Folio 'intrince' — both are rare variants of 'intrinsic.' Kent's speech (TLN 1093-1101) is the scene's most sustained moral argument, and this image is its core.

Kent uses the image to say that flatterers like Oswald have no fixed conviction — they swing their opinions to face whichever way the wind of their master's mood is blowing, denying one moment and affirming the next, always pointing into whoever is in power.

anchor_text: Goose, an I had you upon Sarum plain, / I'd drive ye cackling home to Camelot
summary: Sarum is the old Latin name for Salisbury in Wiltshire, whose nearby chalk downland (Salisbury Plain) was vast, open grazing land. 'Camelot,' the legendary seat of King Arthur, was placed by some traditions at Cadbury Castle in Somerset or at Winchester — not far from Salisbury Plain. Kent is calling Oswald a goose and threatening to herd him cackling across the plain like the farmyard bird he is. The joke also wryly places the play's pagan ancient-British setting: Camelot is this world's nearest city.
detail: The insult 'Goose' answers Oswald's smiling contempt: geese were pastoral commons animals, easily herded, noisy, and stupid. Sarum Plain (Salisbury Plain) was among the most famous open expanses in England — desolate, windswept, appropriate for driving livestock. The Camelot reference is a piece of topographic play: by placing Camelot as the local market-town to which you would drive geese, Kent simultaneously locates the action in legendary Britain (appropriate to the play's pre-Roman setting) and deflates it. Some editors read the line as a comic non-sequitur, its logic being that a goose on Salisbury Plain would naturally waddle toward the only city available in this mythological England.

anchor_text: like the wreath of radiant fire / On flickering Phoebus' front
summary: Phoebus (Latin for 'the bright one') is the sun-god Apollo in his role as the charioteer of the sun. His 'front' is his face or brow, and the 'wreath of radiant fire' on it is the corona, the blazing halo of light around the sun's disc. Kent is parodying Cornwall's power by comparing his great 'aspect' (influence, prestige) to the sun's radiance — making his flattery deliberately over-the-top to mock the idea of flattery itself.
detail: The speech from TLN 1128-1136 is Kent's comic performance of the kind of elaborate courtly compliment he despises: he announces he is going 'out of his dialect' (his plain manner of speaking) and into obsequious flattery, and then produces something so florid it immediately tips into absurdity. 'Under the allowance of your great aspect' borrows the astrological sense of 'aspect' — a great noble's influence was imagined as emanating like planetary rays — and the sun-god simile in the next lines piles on excess. Cornwall correctly senses the mockery and asks 'What mean'st by this?'

anchor_text: None of these rogues and cowards / But Ajax is their fool
summary: Ajax was the greatest brute-force warrior of the Greeks at Troy — physically the mightiest man in the army after Achilles, but famous for his rage and, ultimately, his madness. Kent's point is that every such cowardly rogue and braggart as Oswald models himself on Ajax: they all pretend to the swagger of a great warrior, making even the enormous Ajax look foolish by comparison with their puffed-up posturing.
detail: Ajax (son of Telamon) was the Greek hero second only to Achilles in strength at Troy; in Homer's Iliad he is the great shield-carrying defender. After Achilles died, Ajax and Odysseus competed for Achilles' armour: the other Greeks awarded it to Odysseus, and Ajax, maddened by the slight, slaughtered a flock of sheep thinking them his enemies, then killed himself in shame. His name therefore evoked both supreme physical courage and the destruction of honour through self-delusion — an apt byword for the counterfeit bravado Kent has just witnessed in Oswald. The line is phrased as a double comparison: these cowards and rogues are all imitating Ajax, making the real Ajax (a genuinely great fighter) their unwitting dupe.

sources.name: Homer, Iliad
sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 7-8, 17 (Ajax as the great shield-bearing Greek warrior); Sophocles, Ajax (Ajax's madness and suicide after losing Achilles' armour to Odysseus).

sources.name: Schmidt, Shakespeare-Lexicon
sources.citation: Schmidt, A. Shakespeare-Lexicon, s.v. 'Ajax' (the great Trojan-war warrior, also noted for his rage and madness).

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1148

Homer's Iliad books 7, 8, and 17 do prominently feature Ajax as the great shield-bearing warrior, and Sophocles' Ajax depicts his madness and suicide after losing Achilles' armour to Odysseus; both sources are real and support the claims made.

The claim that cowards and rogues 'model themselves on Ajax' making him their dupe is one reading, but the line more naturally means that even Ajax — the greatest brute-force warrior — would be made to look a fool by comparison with how brazen these cowards are, i.e., their impudence exceeds even Ajax's legendary greatness; the annotation's paraphrase is not wrong but soft-pedals the simpler and more widely accepted reading.

anchor_text: if I were your father's dog, / You should not use me so
summary: Kent argues that even a dog belonging to Lear would have the right to better treatment than he is receiving. In this culture a man's dog was under his protection; to mistreat the king's own dog would be an insult to the king. By placing himself below a dog in Regan's eyes, Kent is sharply inverting the expected social hierarchy to expose how far her contempt for her father extends: if even a dog of Lear's would be better treated, then she is treating a king's loyal servant worse than his dog.
detail: The argument uses a rhetorical figure called a fortiori ('from the stronger') or, in the comparative version, minore ad maius: if the lesser case would be treated better, the greater case should be treated much better. Kent, as Lear's servant and a disguised earl, outranks a dog in every possible register; the fact that he invokes the dog beneath him marks the extremity of the humiliation. Regan's reply — 'Sir, being his knave, I will' — accepts the insult to Lear embedded in Kent's logic without apparently grasping or caring about it, which is its own revelation of her attitude to her father.

sources.name: Onions, Shakespeare Glossary

anchor_text: Fortune, good night: smile once more, turn thy wheel
summary: Fortune was imagined in the classical and medieval tradition as a goddess turning a great wheel — those at the top are flung down, those at the bottom may be lifted up. Sitting in the stocks at the low point of his fortunes, Kent addresses Fortune directly and asks her to turn her wheel so that things may improve. The line is both stoic (he accepts his position) and hopeful (the wheel always turns).
detail: The image of Fortune and her wheel derives from Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy (c. 524 CE), which became one of the most widely read books in medieval and Renaissance Europe and was translated into English by Chaucer and others. In Lear the wheel-image recurs throughout: Edmund will cry 'The wheel is come full circle; I am here' as he dies (5.3), and the Fool invokes Fortune repeatedly. Here Kent, alone and in the stocks, adopts the image with a kind of rueful wit: the scene closes on him reading Cordelia's letter and sleeping, enduring his low point while trusting that Fortune's wheel keeps turning. The tone is characteristically Kentian — patient but not passive.

anchor_text: basest and most poorest shape / That ever penury, in contempt of man, / Brought near to beast
summary: Elizabethan thought pictured creation as a ranked ladder — the 'great chain of being' — with God at the top, then angels, then humans, then animals, then plants. To sink 'near to beast' is to slide down that ladder toward the level of brutes, losing what defines the human: reason and dignity. Edgar chooses the very lowest human form — the naked, filthy, maddened Bedlam beggar — a shape 'penury' (extreme poverty) forces on men who have lost everything.
detail: The phrase 'contempt of man' means contempt for humankind — that is, poverty so absolute it strips away the marks of human dignity and leaves the man barely distinguishable from a beast. The degradation is deliberate and layered: Edgar, a nobleman, will stand closer to the animal kingdom than to his own social rank. The same downward movement obsesses Lear, who on the heath asks what man is 'without... thick-robing fury?' and answers 'bare, forked animal' — the scene where he meets the disguised Edgar. Edgar's self-description here anticipates that question.

anchor_text: Bedlam beggars, who, with roaring voices, / Strike in their numb'd and mortified bare arms / Pins, wooden pricks, nails
summary: Bethlem Royal Hospital in London (corrupted to 'Bedlam') housed the mentally ill. Released or counterfeit inmates roamed the countryside as wandering beggars -- known as 'Tom o' Bedlam' or 'Abram-men' -- soliciting charity with wild cries and, by later accounts, driving pins or skewers into their numbed arms as a display of insensibility to prove they were mad. Edgar plans to impersonate one.
detail: Bethlem Royal Hospital, founded in 1247 and dedicated to the care of the insane by the later medieval period, could hold only a small number of patients; former inmates and impostors alike begged under the name 'Bedlamites,' and 'Abram-men' (from the ward named Abraham) was another name for this wandering class. Thomas Harman's A Caveat for Common Cursitors (1566) describes the Abram-men as feigned madmen who beg; the lurid self-harm with pins and nails is detailed in later rogue-pamphlets (e.g. Dekker's O per se O, 1612). Edgar's list -- pins, wooden pricks, nails, sprigs of rosemary -- draws on this tradition, and the persona gives him cover to move through a countryside where he is proclaimed a traitor.

anchor_text: Poor Turlygod! poor Tom! / That's something yet:--Edgar I nothing am
summary: 'Poor Tom' is the generic name for the wandering Bedlam beggar Edgar is about to become; 'Turlygod' (found only here in Shakespeare) appears to be another name or cry of the same type, though its precise origin is lost. The couplet turns on a radical self-erasure: by taking the identity 'Tom,' Edgar gains 'something' — a survivable disguise — while the man he was, Edgar, becomes 'nothing.' The play puts enormous weight on the word 'nothing': it is what Cordelia says to Lear in 1.1, and it echoes here as the cost of survival.
detail: Editors from Johnson onward have been puzzled by 'Turlygod': it may be a corruption of an Irish or cant term, or a wandering beggar's cry, but no certain source has been found. The Quarto text reads 'Turlygod,' the Folio agrees; it is therefore clearly intentional, not a compositor's error, but its derivation remains uncertain. 'Poor Tom' is the standard type-name for the Bedlam wanderer, drawn from the rogue-literature tradition and from Harsnett's 1603 account of fake exorcism; Edgar will use it throughout Acts 3-4. The phrase 'Edgar I nothing am' collapses a nobleman's name and legal identity into 'nothing' — a nothingness that parallels Lear's own stripping of title, retinue, and shelter.

anchor_text: he wears cruel garters. Horses are tied by the
summary: The Fool puns on 'cruel' (the word also meant a thin crewel wool yarn used for garters) and 'wooden nether-stocks' (stocks, the punishment device, punning on 'stockings'). A man put in the stocks has his legs fastened, as animals are tied by head, neck, or loins — so he wears the cruelest garters of all.
detail: The Fool's joke works on two levels. 'Cruel' sounds like 'crewel,' a coarse worsted thread used to knit garters; and 'nether-stocks' means both the leg-irons of the stocks and ordinary stockings ('nether' = lower). Animals are tied by their strongest part; men, the Fool says, are tied by their legs when they are 'over-lusty at legs' — too eager to run away from those in power. The joke belittles the punishment by domesticating it, even as it underlines Kent's humiliation.

anchor_text: By Jupiter, I swear no
summary: Lear swears by Jupiter (the Roman king of the gods), and Kent immediately counters with Juno (Jupiter's queen). The exchange is typical of the play's pagan ancient-British setting: these characters do not swear by the Christian God but by the Olympian gods of classical antiquity.
detail: King Lear is deliberately set in a pre-Christian Britain where characters invoke Jupiter, Apollo, Hecate, and 'the gods' rather than the God of the Bible. Jupiter (Greek Zeus) was the supreme deity, the god of thunder, oaths, and kingship; Juno was his wife, queen of heaven. Having Lear and Kent swear by opposing Olympian deities gives their exchange a mock-solemn comic formality even as it shows their refusal to yield ground.

anchor_text: Winter's not gone yet, if the wild geese fly that way
summary: The Fool uses a proverbial saying — wild geese flying south signal winter is not over — to mean that trouble has not passed yet. He then drives the point home in a rhyming couplet: fathers with full purses ('bags') get kindness from their children; fathers dressed in rags are ignored. Lear has given away his wealth and is now experiencing the predictable result.
detail: The Fool's strategy throughout the play is to wrap uncomfortable truths in proverbs, jokes, and rhymes. The goose-saying has the force of a weather-omen: Cornwall and Regan's behaviour toward Kent is a sign (like southward-flying geese) that worse cold is coming. The couplet on 'rags' and 'bags' is a plain-spoken inversion of the filial piety Lear expected: money, not blood, is what makes children 'kind' (an Elizabethan word meaning both 'affectionate' and 'natural, fulfilling one's kin-duty').

anchor_text: Fortune, that arrant whore, Ne'er turns the key to th' poor
summary: The Fool invokes the classical figure of Fortune as a prostitute who gives her favours only to the powerful and rich, never to the poor. 'Turns the key' means opens the door — Fortune never lets the poor man in. This directly mirrors Lear's situation: he is losing his followers as his power drains away.
detail: Fortune was imagined in classical and medieval tradition as a goddess who blindly distributed luck by spinning a wheel or opening and closing her door. To call her a 'whore' or 'strumpet' — a favourite Elizabethan epithet — meant she gave her favours to whoever was currently powerful, with no loyalty or justice. The Fool ties this to Lear's loss of retinue: those who 'follow' great men do so only while Fortune's door is open to them. The same figure appears in the Fool's wheel-speech three lines later.

anchor_text: O, how this mother swells up toward my heart! Hysterica passio
summary: 'Hysterica passio' is the Latin name for a medical condition called 'the mother' or 'suffocation of the mother' — a fit of choking or smothering sensation thought to rise from the womb (Latin: uterus) upward to the heart and throat. Lear feels it as a physical rising sensation of grief and rage that threatens to choke him, and he commands it back down.
detail: In Renaissance medicine, 'the mother' (or 'suffocation of the mother,' hysterica passio) was attributed to vapours rising from the uterus. It was considered primarily a woman's condition, which makes Lear's naming of it deeply charged: he is fighting an uncontrollable surge of emotion that he feels as feminizing. The phrase 'thy element's below' commands the feeling back to its proper (lower) place. Shakespeare's source for the medical detail is likely Edward Jorden's A Brief Discourse of a Disease Called the Suffocation of the Mother (1603), published just before the play.

anchor_text: We'll set thee to school to an ant, to teach thee there's no labouring in the winter
summary: The Fool refers to Aesop's fable of the ant and the grasshopper: the ant stores food in summer because it knows winter is coming and there will be nothing to gather. The Fool tells Kent that even an ant could have predicted that following a king stripped of power in the political 'winter' of his fortunes would lead to nothing. A wise servant follows the rising great, not the falling ones.
detail: The ant-and-grasshopper fable (Aesop no. 373 in Perry's index) was a school-text byword for foresight and the wisdom of reading the season. The Fool's advice — 'let go thy hold when a great wheel runs down a hill' — is the same lesson from Fortune's wheel applied to courtly service. Cynically, he recommends following only the ascending great (Fortune's wheel going up), and he admits that only fools and knaves follow the counsel he himself is giving. The speech is the Fool's sharpest commentary on courtiers who abandoned Lear.

anchor_text: Cry to it, nuncle, as the cockney did to the eels when she put 'em i' the paste alive
summary: The Fool tells Lear that crying 'down!' to his swelling heart is as useless as the cook ('cockney' = a soft, city-bred woman here) who shouted at eels to lie still in the pie-crust while she was kneading them in alive. Just as live eels will not stay down no matter how you hit them, Lear's grief will not be ordered back by an act of will. The Fool's companion joke — a man who buttered his horse's hay out of 'pure kindness' — adds a second image of misguided well-meaning.

The image is comic and pathetic together: the Fool diagnoses Lear's futile attempt to govern his own emotions by brute command.

anchor_text: I would divorce me from thy mother's tomb, Sepulchring an adultress
summary: Lear threatens to disown the memory of his dead queen — to 'divorce' himself from her grave — if Regan is not genuinely glad to see him, because her ingratitude would prove she is a bastard (her mother an adultress). The threat is legally and emotionally grotesque: one cannot divorce a corpse. It measures Lear's desperation to believe Regan is loyal by imagining a violent alternative.
detail: The speech reveals how completely Lear has staked his self-image on Regan's loyalty. He frames the hypothetical as a retrospective slander on his dead wife's fidelity — a charge of bastardy aimed at the daughter while ostensibly honouring the marriage. The logic parallels his earlier disinheritance of Cordelia: when reality disappoints him, Lear rewrites the bonds of blood.

anchor_text: she hath tied Sharp-tooth'd unkindness, like a vulture, here
summary: Lear compares Goneril's 'unkindness' to a vulture gnawing at his heart. This alludes to the punishment of the Titan Prometheus, chained to a rock while an eagle (or vulture) ate his liver daily, which grew back each night for the torment to repeat. The image equates Lear with the suffering, bound figure rather than the beneficent one.
detail: Prometheus, who gave fire (knowledge, life) to humanity, was punished by Zeus with eternal torture: chained to a mountain, he endured a bird tearing at his liver each day. The play makes Lear the victim of the very children he raised and endowed, and the vulture-metaphor positions Goneril as an instrument of divine punishment gnawing at the seat of feeling (the heart). The vulture-at-the-heart was a common emblem for gnawing grief or guilt across classical and Renaissance literature.

fact_check_verdicts.note: anchor located deterministically at TLN 1361

Hesiod Theogony 507-616 does contain the Prometheus punishment (eagle eating the liver); Ovid Met. 4.459 does describe Tityus and the vulture in the underworld — both sources genuinely support the imagery of an eternally gnawing bird, though Hesiod specifies an eagle not a vulture (the annotation correctly hedges 'eagle or vulture').

The vulture-at-the-heart as a general emblem of gnawing grief is well attested, but the specific Prometheus identification is a reach: the text says Lear points to his heart (not his liver), and the vulture-at-the-liver punishment belongs to Tityus in Ovid as much as Prometheus — the annotation conflates the two myths; the more parsimonious reading is the common 'vulture of grief' emblem without a single mythological referent.

anchor_text: Nature in you stands on the very verge Of her confine: you should be rul'd and led By some discretion
summary: Regan tells Lear that his human nature ('Nature in you') stands at the very edge ('verge') of its proper boundary — meaning he is at the extreme limit of old age, about to pass beyond the bounds of reason or capacity. She is telling him, bluntly, that he is too old to govern himself and should submit to others' judgment. The line is one of the play's most pointed arguments for stripping Lear of authority.

anchor_text: Age is unnecessary: on my knees I beg That you'll vouchsafe me raiment, bed, and food
summary: Lear performs a bitter mock-submission, kneeling and begging for the barest necessities — clothing, shelter, and food — as Regan asked. It is savage irony: a king should not kneel to his child; and reducing his needs to 'raiment, bed, and food' reduces him to the status of a beggar. 'Age is unnecessary' is the play's sharpest statement of what Regan's position means: old people have no further use.
detail: The kneeling is explicitly theatrical — Lear is parodying the posture of humble petition that Regan demanded when she told him to return to Goneril and apologize. By staging a grotesque parody of it ('Dear daughter, I confess that I am old'), he exposes the degradation her demand actually requires. 'Unnecessary' does not simply mean 'not needed right now'; it means 'without function, superfluous.' The word quietly anticipates the later 'O, reason not the need' speech.

In Elizabethan medicine 'fen-suck'd fogs' and bad air ('miasma') were believed to carry disease and blast crops or bodies they touched.

The phrase 'fen-suck'd fogs, drawn by the powerful sun' (TLN 1399) makes the image explicit: the sun sucks up the foul vapour from the fenlands, which then falls as blighting mist. The combination of 'taking airs,' lightning, and fog stages an escalating supernatural curse on Goneril.

anchor_text: If you do love old men, if your sweet sway Allow obedience, if yourselves are old, Make it your cause

anchor_text: I abjure all roofs, and choose To wage against the enmity o' the air; To be a comrade with the wolf and owl

anchor_text: Or rather a disease that's in my flesh, Which I must needs call mine: thou art a boil, A plague sore, an embossed carbuncle

anchor_text: Made you my guardians, my depositaries; But kept a reservation to be follow'd
summary: 'Depositaries' (or depositories) are trustees — people to whom property is entrusted for safekeeping. 'Reservation' means a specified right or condition held back in a legal transfer. Lear reminds Regan that when he gave his daughters the kingdom he retained ('reserved') the right to keep his hundred knights. He is making a legal argument: he fulfilled the gift but kept one specified condition, which they are now violating.

The scene's whole movement is from political negotiation to emotional disintegration.

anchor_text: O, reason not the need: our basest beggars Are in the poorest thing superfluous
summary: Lear argues that you cannot reduce human dignity to bare physical necessity. Even the poorest beggar has at least one thing he possesses beyond sheer animal need. If you strip away everything that exceeds strict necessity, then a lady's gorgeous clothing (which provides no extra warmth over a plain garment) has no justification either — yet Regan wears it. The argument is that 'need' means more than biological survival; it includes dignity, status, and the social marks of humanity.
detail: The speech is among the most philosophically dense in the play. Lear's point is that the daughters' logic — what do you 'need' more than a specified number of knights? — would, if consistently applied, reduce all human life to animal existence. Regan herself wears clothes 'which scarcely keeps thee warm': a gorgeous gown that is chosen for social display, not survival. Therefore the need for display, for ceremony, for the marks of one's station, is as real as the need for warmth. He is defending the principle that the retinue is not about physical comfort but about what it means to be a king, or a man.

The cruelty of the scene is that Lear is crying or about to cry even as he denies it.

anchor_text: O, sir, to wilful men The injuries that they themselves procure Must be their schoolmasters
summary: After Lear storms out into the coming storm, Regan uses a sententious moral saying ('wilful men must learn from the harms they bring on themselves') to justify shutting the doors against him. The sentence has the form of a proverb or moral maxim, which gives it an air of wisdom while excusing her cruelty as his own fault. It is one of the play's clearest examples of cold policy dressed in the language of moral correction.

anchor_text: his little world of man to outscorn
summary: The phrase 'little world of man' draws on the ancient idea of the microcosm: the human body was thought to mirror the structure of the whole universe (the macrocosm), so a storm raging inside a person corresponded to a storm raging outside in nature. Lear striving against the tempest is therefore not just a mad old man in bad weather — he is a cosmos at war with itself.
detail: The microcosm-macrocosm analogy — 'man is a little world' — was a commonplace of ancient philosophy (Aristotle, Physics 8.2) and Renaissance natural philosophy. It held that every element in the human body (the four humours, the vital spirits, the reason that was meant to govern the passions) had its counterpart in the elements of the universe. A king, moreover, was the microcosm of the body politic: his disordered mind and the storm on the heath are the same disorder expressing itself at two scales. The Gentleman's phrasing 'strives in his little world of man to outscorn / The to-and-fro-conflicting wind and rain' makes the competition equal — Lear's inner storm and the outer storm are matched opponents, neither able to defeat the other. This is the play's first explicit statement of the storm-as-inner-state metaphor that will dominate the Act 3 scenes.

summary: 'Cub-drawn' means drained dry by her nursing cubs — a she-bear so exhausted from suckling that she would normally curl up and stay hidden even in bad weather. Only Lear, stripped of shelter by his daughters, is still out in it, bareheaded.

The logic is that a nursing bear, depleted of nourishment, would be ravenously hungry and therefore inclined to roam and forage — yet even she shelters from this storm. The progression in lines 1570-1572 is from the bear (the most ferocious of European land predators) to the lion, to the 'belly-pinched' (starving) wolf: in each case the hungriest, most dangerous animal seeks shelter. Lear, who has been stripped of all protection and provision by his daughters, is more exposed and more suffering than any of them.

anchor_text: fool, who labours to out-jest / His heart-struck injuries
summary: 'Out-jest' means to overcome or drive away by making jokes — to jest something out of existence. 'Heart-struck injuries' are wounds aimed directly at the heart, the injuries dealt to Lear by his daughters' cruelty. The Fool's whole effort is to joke Lear out of his grief, but the Gentleman implies the task is beyond him: the injuries are too deep for humor to cure. The line also confirms the Fool is still at Lear's side on the heath.
detail: The verb 'out-jest' is a Shakespearean coinage. In the Fool's role, licensed jesters were expected to defuse dangerous emotions through wit and wordplay — the court fool traditionally had permission to say what no one else dared, often using humor to expose hard truths and ease tensions. That the Fool 'labours' to do this signals strenuous, effortful comedy rather than easy wit, and the phrase implies he is failing: you do not 'labour' at something you are succeeding in. 'Heart-struck' is another compound Shakespeare seems to have coined; it distinguishes the daughters' cruelty from ordinary griefs by specifying that the blow lands at the emotional and vital center of the man.

anchor_text: their great stars / Throne and set high
summary: Kent says Albany and Cornwall have servants who are French spies, because who in power does not? — 'who have not, that their great stars / Throne and set high?' The phrase 'great stars throne and set high' means the powerful stars of a person's birth-chart that have placed them in their high position. In Shakespeare's world, a person's rank and fortune were widely believed to be determined by the configuration of stars at their birth.
detail: Renaissance astrology, which was mainstream learning rather than fringe belief, held that the planets and stars at a person's birth 'throned' them — set them in their destined rank. Kent's aside ('as who have not, that their great stars / Throne and set high?') is a parenthetical observation that great men almost inevitably have spies around them, built in by the logic of power. The word 'throne' is used as a verb — the stars do the enthroning, as if the social hierarchy were a natural consequence of celestial arrangement. This is the vocabulary of the same belief that Gloucester invokes (1.2) with his 'late eclipses' speech, and that Edmund scorns. The passive relationship between great men and their stars — they are set high, they do not simply rise — is characteristic of the play's older, more fatalistic characters.

anchor_text: snuffs and packings of the dukes
summary: 'Snuffs' means resentments or sullen displeasures — the word comes from 'snuff' in the sense of taking offense, as in the phrase 'take it in snuff' (to take offense at something). 'Packings' means secret plots or conspiracies. Kent is telling the Gentleman that France's spies have been watching either the angry quarrels between Albany and Cornwall or their behind-the-scenes scheming — or possibly something even more serious than either.

Both words were current in Elizabethan English. 'In snuff' as a phrase for taking offense appears elsewhere in Shakespeare (Love's Labour's Lost 5.2.22; 1 Henry IV 3.1.217). 'Packing' in the sense of secret plotting or underhand dealing is common across the plays. Kent's syntax keeps both possible readings open — it is not clear whether the dukes are rivals to each other or jointly plotting against something else — which is part of the deliberately tangled, compressed intelligence briefing he is delivering.

anchor_text: from France there comes a power / Into this scatter'd kingdom
summary: A 'power' is a military force — an army. 'Scatter'd' means split apart, in pieces, dis-ordered. Kent is revealing to the Gentleman that a French army has already landed in England, slipping into the best ports while the kingdom is too fractured by its internal quarrels to notice or resist. This is the first mention that Cordelia's France has intervened militarily, and it is the crisis that makes Kent need a messenger to reach Dover.

'Scatter'd' carries the weight of the play's opening catastrophe: Lear's division of the kingdom into competing territories has left it without a unified command or loyalty, 'scatter'd' among Albany, Cornwall, and Goneril and Regan's rival ambitions. The phrase 'wise in our negligence' (line 1592) is particularly pointed: the French have not needed to be cunning — they have simply watched England neglect its own defenses while its rulers quarrel. The scene here prefigures the arrival of the French army that will be one of the central plot engines of Acts 4 and 5.
